title: Red-flag triage: how fast does this need a doctor?
objective: Given a short account from a client or family member who is taking psychiatric medicine, decide how quickly a medical professional must see them (routine, discuss with the prescriber soon, or urgent same-day medical review), name the cues that drove the decision, and state the psychologist's next action without giving medical advice.

bookRef.book: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry
bookRef.chapter: Ch 1 (adverse effects; clozapine), Ch 2 (lithium; lamotrigine), Ch 3 (serotonin syndrome; withdrawal; hyponatraemia), Ch 5-7 (special groups), Ch 11 (smoking)

content.instructions: Read each message. Choose one: ROUTINE (note it, mention at the next planned review, no extra contact needed), DISCUSS WITH PRESCRIBER SOON (contact the prescriber or care team within days, sooner if it gets worse; the client should not change the medicine on their own), or URGENT SAME-DAY MEDICAL REVIEW (the person needs medical assessment today; if they are very unwell, confused, collapsing, fitting or struggling to breathe, call emergency services now). You are not diagnosing. You are deciding speed. When in doubt, go one level faster.

items.vignette: Imran's sister calls before his session. Imran, 24, has schizophrenia and his antipsychotic was increased last week. Since yesterday he has been very stiff, sweating heavily, feels hot to touch and is not making sense. He was talking normally three days ago.
items.explanation: Stiffness, fever, sweating and a change in consciousness soon after an antipsychotic change is the classic pattern of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It is rare (Maudsley gives incidence estimates of 0.11-0.16%, p. 131), but it can be fatal. Recent or rapid dose increase and dehydration are listed risk factors (Table 1.19, p. 132). This needs emergency medical care today, not a therapy session.
items.psychologistAction: Advise the family to take him to an emergency department now (or call an ambulance), and tell them to bring his medicine list. Inform the prescriber and the team. Document.

items.vignette: Kavita, 38, takes an SSRI for depression. Two days ago another doctor added a medicine for her migraines. Today in session she is shaky and restless, has jerky leg movements, is sweating, says her heart is racing and has had diarrhoea since morning. Her pupils look large.
cues: a second medicine added recently by a different prescriber
items.explanation: This picture fits serotonin syndrome, which is more likely when two serotonergic medicines are combined (Maudsley p. 337). Agitation, myoclonus, tremor, dilated pupils and sweating fall in the moderate band of Maudsley's severity table (p. 337). Severe cases can progress to high fever, rigidity and confusion. Moderate features already need same-day medical assessment.
items.psychologistAction: Stop the session, explain calmly that this may be a medicine reaction that needs a doctor today, and arrange urgent medical review (emergency department if symptoms are worsening). Tell the team about both prescribers.

items.vignette: Arun, 34, started an SSRI five days ago. He says he has felt a little queasy after the morning tablet and slightly jittery, but both are already easing. No fever, no shaking, no diarrhoea. His mood is unchanged and he has no thoughts of self-harm.
items.explanation: Mild nausea and some jitteriness are common in the first days of an SSRI and often settle. Nothing here suggests serotonin syndrome (no tremor, jerks, sweating or fever). This is a good moment for psychoeducation: early side effects often come before benefit, which can take weeks.
items.psychologistAction: Normalise, encourage him to mention it at his planned review, and tell him what would need faster contact (worsening restlessness, shaking, fever, or any thoughts of self-harm). Keep screening risk at each session.

items.vignette: Mrs Fernandes, 61, has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for many years. Three weeks ago her GP started a 'water tablet' for blood pressure. She now has a coarse tremor, has been vomiting, walks unsteadily and seems muddled on the phone.
items.explanation: Diuretics, especially thiazides, reduce lithium clearance, and Maudsley notes levels usually rise within 10 days of a thiazide being started (p. 253). GI upset with coarse tremor, unsteadiness and confusion is the typical picture of lithium toxicity (p. 250). It can progress to seizures and coma (p. 250-251).
items.psychologistAction: Same-day emergency medical assessment. Tell the family to bring all her medicines, including the new tablet. Inform the psychiatrist and the GP.
items.overlapNote: Existing cases use ibuprofen (sc-pharm-1) and a stomach bug ('summer of lithium'). This item uses a diuretic trigger to avoid duplication.

items.vignette: Dev, 45, has been well on lithium for six years. He mentions in passing that his hands have always had a slight fine shake when he holds a cup. It has not changed, the team knows about it, and he has no other symptoms.
items.explanation: A fine tremor is a recognised common side effect of lithium (Maudsley p. 250). What matters is change: a tremor that becomes coarse, or comes with vomiting, unsteadiness or confusion, is a toxicity warning.
items.psychologistAction: Note it. Remind him what change would be a warning sign. He can raise it at routine monitoring.

items.vignette: Salma, 29, is well on lithium. She tells you she plans to start a strict low-salt diet to lose weight and will also be fasting through long, hot summer days next month. She has not told her psychiatrist.
items.explanation: Most risk factors for lithium toxicity involve sodium or fluid balance, for example low-salt diets and dehydration (Maudsley p. 251). Nothing is wrong yet, but the plan changes her risk. The prescriber should know before she starts so that monitoring can be adjusted.
items.psychologistAction: Explain the link without alarm, support her to contact her psychiatrist before starting, and agree that she will tell you if she feels unwell. Respect the reasons behind the fast and the diet. Do not argue her out of them.

items.vignette: Tarun, 52, on lithium, says that over the past few months he is always thirsty and gets up three or four times a night to pass urine. He otherwise feels fine and his mood is stable.
items.explanation: Thirst and passing a lot of urine are known lithium effects on the kidney (Maudsley p. 250). Long-term kidney function is monitored on lithium. This is not an emergency, but it should be reported, not just put up with. Drinking less to avoid night-time trips could make dehydration and toxicity more likely.
items.psychologistAction: Encourage him to tell the prescriber this week and to keep drinking normally. Escalate to urgent if vomiting, unsteadiness or confusion appear.

items.vignette: Ramesh, 31, started clozapine six weeks ago. His mother says he has had a sore throat and fever since last night and now has painful mouth ulcers. He is tired but talking normally.
cues: sore throat and mouth ulcers (signs of infection)
items.explanation: Any sign of infection on clozapine (fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, flu-like illness) must be checked the same day for a dangerously low white cell count. Maudsley reports agranulocytosis in 0.4% of clozapine patients (p. 222). The risk is highest early and falls after the first year. The team will arrange an urgent blood count.
items.psychologistAction: Contact the clozapine team or prescriber today and make sure he is seen for a blood test today. Do not wait for the next routine blood test.

items.vignette: Joseph, 40, has been on clozapine for two years. In session he looks uncomfortable and holds his stomach. He has not opened his bowels for five days, feels bloated, and vomited this morning. He thought it was 'just gas'.
items.explanation: Clozapine slows the gut. Constipation affects more than 30% of patients, and when it is severe the case fatality is around 20-30% (Maudsley p. 232). It can happen at any time in treatment. Vomiting and pain with no bowel opening suggest possible obstruction, which is an emergency.
items.psychologistAction: Same-day medical assessment (emergency department if pain is severe). Tell the team. Afterwards, add bowel habit to your routine check-in questions with him.

items.vignette: Faisal, 36, on clozapine for a year, stopped smoking ten days ago after a chest infection scare. Proud of himself, he mentions that he is now sleeping most of the day, feels very groggy and had 'a few sudden jerks' in his arms yesterday.
items.explanation: Smoking speeds up the liver enzyme (CYP1A2) that clears clozapine, so smoking can reduce clozapine levels by up to 50%. After stopping, enzyme activity roughly halves every 2 days, so levels can rise sharply (Maudsley p. 856). Nicotine replacement does not prevent this (p. 856). Heavy sedation and jerks suggest the level may now be too high.
items.psychologistAction: Arrange same-day medical review and tell the prescriber he has stopped smoking. Praise the quit attempt. The problem is the unplanned change, not the quitting.

items.vignette: Neha, 27, on clozapine, has been working with you on motivation and tells you she has set a date to quit smoking next month. She feels well.
items.explanation: Quitting is a good health goal, and the prescriber needs to plan for it because clozapine levels rise when smoking stops (Maudsley p. 856). Informing the team before the quit date lets them plan monitoring.
items.psychologistAction: Support the quit plan, and help her tell the prescriber before the quit date. Agree to watch for sleepiness or jerks after she stops.

items.vignette: Vikram, 23, started clozapine three weeks ago. He says he has had a 'flu' for two days with fever, feels his heart pounding even at rest, gets breathless on the stairs and had chest pain this morning.
cues: fast heart rate, breathlessness, chest pain
items.explanation: Myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart muscle, is a known clozapine risk. It is most likely in the first 6-8 weeks (median 3 weeks, Maudsley p. 223) and is potentially fatal (p. 222). Symptoms include fever, flu-like illness, a fast heart rate, breathlessness and chest pain (p. 223).
items.psychologistAction: Emergency medical assessment now; chest pain with breathlessness means calling emergency services. Inform the clozapine team.

items.vignette: Anil, 33, has been on clozapine for four months and is doing much better. He is embarrassed to tell you that his pillow is wet with saliva every morning and he has started skipping evening doses because of it.
cues: now missing doses because of a side effect
items.explanation: Hypersalivation is a common clozapine side effect (Maudsley section at p. 227). It is not dangerous in itself, but it is distressing and is already affecting adherence. Missed doses matter because restarting clozapine after a break needs medical advice (p. 207).
items.psychologistAction: Thank him for telling you. Explain that it is a known, manageable side effect and help him raise it with the prescriber this week, including the skipped doses.

items.vignette: Pooja, 26, began lamotrigine for bipolar depression about three weeks ago. Today she has a spreading red rash, a temperature, sore eyes and painful sores inside her mouth. Some patches look like blisters.
items.explanation: Lamotrigine can cause serious rashes, including rarely the life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome (Stahl p. 352; Maudsley p. 289). A rash with fever, mucous membrane involvement (mouth, eyes) or blistering is an emergency.
items.psychologistAction: Same-day emergency medical review. Tell her not to take another dose until a doctor has seen her, and inform the prescriber.

items.vignette: Meera, 35, has been stable on lamotrigine for a year. She ran out of tablets and missed about ten days. She has a new strip and tells you she will 'just restart tonight where I left off'.
cues: plans to restart at her previous full amount
items.explanation: Rash risk with lamotrigine is linked to how fast the dose rises (Maudsley p. 289). After a long gap, restarting at the old full amount can act like a fast increase. Only the prescriber can advise how to restart. This needs contact before tonight's dose, so 'soon' here means today.
items.psychologistAction: Ask her to contact the prescriber before taking it tonight. Do not advise on the dose yourself. Use the moment to explore what led to running out.

items.vignette: Mrs Iyer, 78, started an SSRI two weeks ago and also takes a diuretic. Her daughter says she has become confused, nauseous and unsteady, and fell in the bathroom last night.
items.explanation: Low sodium (hyponatraemia) is a known antidepressant effect, usually in the first 30 days (median 11 days, Maudsley p. 393). It is highest risk in the first 2-4 weeks, and older age, female sex and diuretics are key risk factors (p. 394). Confusion and falls suggest it may be significant. Maudsley advises urgent specialist care when sodium is below 125 mmol/L because of the risk of seizures and coma (p. 395). Only a blood test can tell.
items.psychologistAction: Same-day medical review for a sodium test. Do not assume the confusion is 'just dementia' or depression. Inform the prescriber.

items.vignette: Mr Bose, 71, started an antidepressant three weeks ago. He mentions headaches and mild nausea this week. He is alert, walking normally and thinking clearly.
items.explanation: Headache and nausea can be early, mild signs of low sodium (Maudsley p. 394-395), and he is in the highest-risk window and age group. He is not in danger today, but a sodium check should not wait for his next routine appointment.
items.psychologistAction: Contact the prescriber within a day or two about a blood test. Tell him and his family that confusion, unsteadiness or a fall means going straight to a doctor.

items.vignette: Rohan, 20, started an antipsychotic ten days ago. He cannot sit for more than a minute, paces the room, and says the restlessness inside is unbearable: 'If this is how it's going to feel, I'd rather be dead.'
items.explanation: This looks like akathisia: subjective unease plus motor restlessness after an antipsychotic (Maudsley p. 114; Stahl p. 169). It is common, for example 57% with haloperidol in one first-episode analysis (Maudsley p. 114), and very distressing. An association with suicidal ideation has been postulated (p. 114). The death statement makes this a same-day risk and medical issue.
items.psychologistAction: Do a risk assessment now, following your service's suicide protocol. Contact the prescriber today and name the suspected cause (the recent medicine and restlessness), so it is not recorded as 'agitation from psychosis'.

items.vignette: Lata, 56, has taken an antipsychotic for many years. Her husband has noticed over several months that she makes chewing and lip-smacking movements and her tongue moves in her mouth. She is not bothered by it and is otherwise well.
cues: slowly developing involuntary mouth and tongue movements
items.explanation: This suggests tardive dyskinesia, a late movement side effect. Stahl estimates about 5% per year with older drugs, about 25% by 5 years, and a higher risk in older people (p. 170). It is not an emergency, but early recognition matters because the prescriber may review the treatment.
items.psychologistAction: Encourage the couple to report it to the prescriber in the next week or two. Be sensitive to stigma, because visible movements can affect social confidence.

items.vignette: Sunita, 30, started an antipsychotic four months ago and has gained a lot of weight. In the last few weeks she is always thirsty, passing urine often and feels tired. She is alert and eating normally.
cues: thirst, frequent urination, tiredness (possible raised blood sugar)
items.explanation: Several antipsychotics raise weight, lipids and blood sugar (Stahl p. 198-201; Maudsley p. 153). Thirst, frequent urination and fatigue can mean new diabetes, which needs a blood test soon. Stahl notes rare but life-threatening diabetic emergencies (p. 199). Vomiting, drowsiness or confusion would make it urgent.
items.psychologistAction: Contact the prescriber or GP this week for a glucose test. Explore how the weight change is affecting her, because it is a common reason people stop medicine.

items.vignette: Ishaan, 32, stopped his antidepressant suddenly two days ago because he 'felt fine'. Now he is dizzy, nauseous and irritable, and feels 'electric shocks' in his head when he moves his eyes. He has no thoughts of self-harm.
items.explanation: Rapid onset after stopping, with new physical and sensory symptoms such as dizziness and zaps, points to withdrawal (discontinuation) symptoms rather than relapse (Maudsley p. 343). Maudsley gives a weighted average incidence of 56% across studies (p. 344). They are not dangerous here, but they are unpleasant, and the prescriber can advise.
items.psychologistAction: Explain that this is a known reaction to stopping suddenly, not a sign he is 'addicted' or relapsing. Help him contact the prescriber within a day or two. Escalate if mood drops sharply or risk appears.

items.vignette: Aanya, 16, began an SSRI for depression ten days ago. Her mother says she is newly agitated, pacing at night, and today told her she has been thinking about ending her life, which she had never said before.
items.explanation: Maudsley notes a small increased risk of suicidal thinking with antidepressants in young people, especially early on (p. 545), and stresses that untreated depression also carries suicide risk. New suicidal ideation with agitation is a same-day safety matter.
items.psychologistAction: Same-day risk assessment and safety planning with her and her parent. Contact the prescriber today. Do not tell her to stop the medicine; that is a medical decision.

items.vignette: Ritu, 31, on a mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder, has just found out she is about six weeks pregnant. She tells you she threw away all her tablets this morning 'to protect the baby'.
items.explanation: Maudsley lists 'the risks from stopping medication abruptly' and the impact of untreated illness among the topics a pregnant woman should discuss, alongside drug risks (p. 681). It also advises considering a specialist perinatal referral (p. 681). Her instinct is protective and understandable, but the decision needs a prompt joint review. Within days, not at the next routine visit.
items.psychologistAction: Validate her concern, avoid blame, and help her get an early appointment with the prescriber (and a perinatal service if available). Watch for early signs of relapse. Escalate to urgent if mood symptoms appear.

items.vignette: Shalini, 28, has bipolar disorder and gave birth five days ago. Her partner says she has hardly slept for three nights, is talking fast, believes the nurses swapped her baby, and is not making sense at times.
items.explanation: Women with bipolar disorder have a high risk of postpartum psychotic relapse; Maudsley cites around one in five (p. 681). New delusions and confusion within days of birth are a psychiatric emergency for mother and baby.
items.psychologistAction: Same-day emergency psychiatric assessment. Make sure the baby is safely cared for by another adult in the meantime.

items.vignette: Mr Khanna, 82, has dementia and was given an antipsychotic for distress at night. His son calls: this afternoon his father's face drooped on one side, his speech became slurred, and his right arm went weak.
cues: sudden face droop, slurred speech, arm weakness
items.explanation: These are stroke signs, and every minute counts. Maudsley notes older people are more prone to stroke with antipsychotics (p. 601). Whatever the cause, sudden one-sided weakness or speech change needs emergency services immediately.
items.psychologistAction: Tell the son to call an ambulance now. Inform the team afterwards.

items.vignette: Mrs D'Souza, 76, was recently given a sleeping tablet. She says she sleeps better but feels 'wobbly' getting up at night to use the toilet and nearly fell twice this week. No injury.
items.explanation: Older people show an exaggerated response to CNS-active drugs such as benzodiazepines, and blood-pressure effects make falls more likely (Maudsley p. 601). Two near-falls are a warning before an injury happens.
items.psychologistAction: Contact the prescriber this week. Meanwhile, discuss simple night-time safety (a light on the way to the toilet, getting up slowly). Consider CBT for insomnia as a longer-term option.

items.vignette: Gaurav, 41, two months into an SSRI, says his mood is clearly better but he has less interest in sex and finds it harder to climax. He asks if this is normal and whether he should stop the tablets.
items.explanation: Sexual side effects are common with serotonergic antidepressants (Maudsley section at p. 404) and are a frequent hidden reason for stopping. It is not urgent, but it should be raised openly with the prescriber because options exist, and stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms (p. 343).
items.psychologistAction: Normalise and encourage him to raise it at his next review (sooner if he is about to stop). Ask him not to stop on his own.

content.debrief: Pattern to remember: (1) Unwell body plus psychiatric medicine (fever, rigidity, confusion, vomiting, chest pain, rash with fever, infection on clozapine, no bowel movement on clozapine) means same day. (2) A change that raises risk but no symptoms yet (planned quit smoking, low-salt diet, pregnancy, missed doses) means tell the prescriber soon, before the change. (3) Known, stable, mild effects mean routine, as long as you have said what would make it faster.

reviewFlags: Clinical sign-off required before release: triage levels are teaching defaults and must match local service pathways.
Emergency numbers and clozapine-monitoring contacts in India vary by service; localise the 'who to call' wording.
Items t18 and t22 involve suicidal statements: cross-link to the suicide module risk protocol and review together.
Item t23 deliberately does not name valproate's specific risks (taught in stabilisers 1.2); check consistency.
No doses, levels or titration advice appear; the only laboratory figure (sodium below 125 mmol/L) is cited to Maudsley p. 395 in an explanation, not used for student decisions.

title: Synapse lab: reuptake and the agonist dial
objective: Predict and explain what happens to transmitter level in the gap and to the receiving cell's signal when a reuptake blocker, full agonist, partial agonist, antagonist or inverse agonist is added, and explain why a partial agonist can raise or lower the signal depending on the starting state.

bookRef.chapter: Ch 1 Chemical Neurotransmission; Ch 2 Transporters, Receptors, and Enzymes

content.scene: One sending terminal, a gap, and one receiving cell with five receptors. A transporter ('recycling pump') on the sending side pulls transmitter back. A 'signal meter' on the receiving cell shows 0-100. The natural transmitter is drawn as round tokens; drugs are drawn as distinct shapes. Visuals must be VIBHA originals (do not trace Stahl figures).

baseline.label: Normal firing
baseline.caption: Transmitter is released, some binds, the pump recycles the rest.

controls.label: How much the sending cell is firing

states.caption: The pump is jammed, so transmitter lingers in the gap and keeps reaching receptors. This is how SSRIs start (Stahl ch 2, 31-34).
A pump blocker can only keep what is released. If little is released, the boost is small.
A full agonist switches the receptor fully on whatever the natural transmitter is doing.
The antagonist sits in the receptor but does not switch it on, and stops transmitter getting in. The signal falls to near the receptor's resting level.
With little transmitter around, blocking makes little difference: an antagonist only matters when there is something to block.
When transmitter is high, the partial agonist pushes out the full-strength natural transmitter and replaces it with a weaker 'on', so the signal goes DOWN.
When transmitter is low, the same drug adds some 'on', so the signal goes UP. Same drug, opposite direction, which is why partial agonists are described as stabilising (Stahl ch 2, 42-43).
Some receptors have a little activity even when empty. An inverse agonist turns that background activity off, going below an antagonist (Stahl ch 2, 44).

content.analogyVibha: Think of the receptor as a ceiling fan with a regulator. The natural transmitter turns it to full. A full agonist also turns it to full. An antagonist puts a cover over the switch so nobody can turn it. A partial agonist is a regulator that can only reach speed 2 of 5: in a hot room with the fan at 5 it slows things down; in a still room it gets air moving. An inverse agonist stops even the slight drift the fan has on its own.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Firing is HIGH. You add a partial agonist. Will the signal go up or down?
predictThenReveal.why: It replaces the stronger natural transmitter with a weaker one.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Firing is LOW. You add an antagonist. Big change or small?
predictThenReveal.why: There was little transmitter to block.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Why does an SSRI raise serotonin in the gap without the cell releasing more?
predictThenReveal.answer: It slows recycling, so released serotonin stays longer.

content.clinicLink: When a client says 'the tablet adds serotonin to my brain', you can correct it gently: it helps the brain keep and reuse what it already releases. Aripiprazole-type medicines are partial agonists, which is why they act differently from older antipsychotics (Stahl ch 5, 189-193).

reviewFlags: Signal values (0-100) are illustrative units for animation, not measured quantities; label them as such on screen.
Overlaps with brain 1.1 text (key/lock analogy) and CURRICULUM_MAP row 127; this activity is the planned simulation, so link rather than duplicate.
Original analogy (fan regulator); do not reuse Stahl's light/dimmer analogy (Stahl ch 2, 43) or redraw his icons.

title: The occupancy window: why more is not better
objective: Explain, without any doses, how the share of D2 receptors blocked relates to antipsychotic benefit and to movement side effects and raised prolactin, and use this to explain to a client why 'a stronger dose' is not always better.

bookRef.chapter: Ch 5 Targeting Dopamine and Serotonin Receptors

content.scene: A strip of 10 D2 receptors in two places side by side: an 'emotion and meaning' area (mesolimbic) and a 'movement' area (nigrostriatal). A single slider sets the share of receptors blocked (0-100%), which is identical in both areas. Three meters: symptom relief, movement side-effect risk, prolactin effect.

states.caption: Too few receptors blocked for a reliable antipsychotic effect.
The usual target zone: Stahl describes drugs being dosed so that at least 60-80% of D2 receptors are occupied (p. 201).
Blocking more adds side effects without adding benefit: stiffness, tremor, restlessness (akathisia), dystonia (Stahl ch 5, 165-170).

With a partial agonist, the receptors are never fully silenced, so even high occupancy leaves some signal; motor effects are generally fewer (Stahl ch 5, 192), though akathisia still occurs (e.g., 18% with aripiprazole in one first-episode analysis, Maudsley p. 114).
Many newer drugs also block a serotonin receptor that releases a little dopamine in the movement area, softening motor effects (Stahl ch 5, 183-184).

checks.q: A client says, 'My voices are still there, so I'll double my tablets.' Using the window, what would you explain?
checks.model: Past a point, more blockade adds side effects but not benefit. Changing the dose is the prescriber's decision, and persistent voices are worth reviewing together.

checks.q: Why can the same blockade relieve hallucinations and also cause stiffness?
checks.model: The drug cannot choose where it acts; it blocks D2 in emotion and movement pathways alike.

reviewFlags: Percentages are Stahl's stated occupancy convention (p. 195, 201); they are a teaching model and vary by drug and person.
Already stated as a fact in antipsychotics 1.1 (60-80%); this activity adds the interactive concept, not new facts.
Ensure no dose numbers appear anywhere in the UI.

title: Why weeks? The antidepressant timeline
objective: Explain to a client in plain language why serotonin levels change within hours of starting an SSRI but benefit usually takes weeks, using the autoreceptor-desensitisation model, and say why early side effects can come before benefit.

content.scene: A serotonin cell body (with its own 'brake' receptors, 5HT1A autoreceptors) connected to a terminal and a receiving cell. A timeline scrubber: Day 1, Week 1, Weeks 2-4, Week 6+.

states.caption: The cell fires at its usual rate.
Blocking the pump raises serotonin first around the cell body, which presses the cell's own brake. So the net effect where it matters is small at first (Stahl p. 290-291).
Serotonin rises in other body systems quickly, so side effects like nausea can start before any mood benefit.
With constant stimulation, the brake receptors become less sensitive. The cell fires more freely and more serotonin reaches the terminal (Stahl p. 291-292).
Receiving cells adapt too. This slow timing matches the delayed clinical effect; it is a hypothesis, and other ideas such as neuroplasticity are also discussed (Stahl p. 266-267).

scriptBuilder.task: Drag phrases into a 3-sentence explanation for a client who says 'It's been 5 days and nothing has changed except I feel sick.'
goodPhrases: the medicine works on the brain's own brakes, and they take a few weeks to adjust
feeling sick early is common and often settles
please don't stop suddenly; talk to your doctor if it's hard to bear
trapPhrases: it adds serotonin you are missing
if you don't feel better in a week it isn't working
double up to speed it up

reviewFlags: Present the mechanism as Stahl's explanatory model, not settled fact (evidence: established, details debated).
antidepressants 1.2 already states the delay; this adds the visual and the client script. Check wording against that section.
Timeline labels are approximate and illustrative; not a prediction for individual clients.

title: Four look-alike emergencies
objective: Distinguish neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity and anticholinergic toxicity by medicine history, speed of onset and key signs, while recognising that all four need same-day medical care.

bookRef.book: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry
bookRef.chapter: Ch 1 NMS; Ch 2 Lithium; Ch 3 Switching (serotonin syndrome)

comparisonGrid.NMS: Antipsychotic, especially after a start, increase or rapid change (Maudsley p. 132)
comparisonGrid.SS: Serotonergic medicine, often two together or a recent addition (p. 337)
comparisonGrid.Lithium: Lithium plus dehydration, illness, low salt or an interacting medicine (p. 251-254)
comparisonGrid.Anticholinergic: Medicines with strong anticholinergic action, often several at once (Stahl p. 169)

cases.vignette: Day 3 after a second serotonergic medicine was added: anxious, sweating, jerking legs, diarrhoea.
cases.why: Fast onset after a serotonergic combination; jerks and diarrhoea (Maudsley p. 337).

cases.vignette: Gradual over several days after an antipsychotic increase: stiff as a board, hot, sweating, drifting in and out.
cases.why: Rigidity, fever and fluctuating consciousness after an antipsychotic change (Maudsley p. 132).

cases.vignette: Long-term mood-stabiliser user after a week of diarrhoea in a heatwave: vomiting, big shaky tremor, staggering, muddled.
cases.why: Fluid loss is a key trigger; GI plus coarse tremor plus ataxia plus confusion (Maudsley p. 250-251).

cases.vignette: Older man on several medicines including one for bladder spasm and an old-style antidepressant: dry mouth, hot dry skin, cannot pass urine, confused and picking at the air.
cases.why: Dry, hot skin and urinary retention with confusion: muscarinic blockade (Stahl p. 169).

content.takeaway: You do not need to settle the label. Every one of these is 'unwell and on medicine': same-day medical care. Getting the likely label right helps you tell the doctor what changed.

reviewFlags: antidepressants 3.1 already has an SS-versus-NMS table and MCQ; this activity extends it to four conditions. Avoid duplicating that MCQ.
Anticholinergic toxicity features are general clinical knowledge supported by Stahl p. 169 (muscarinic blockade effects); clinical reviewer to confirm grid wording.
Onset-speed contrasts are typical patterns, not rules.

title: Akathisia or anxiety?
objective: Tell drug-induced akathisia apart from anxiety, psychotic agitation and restless legs by timing, the inner urge to move, the movement pattern and context, and explain why the distinction matters for risk and for the therapeutic relationship.

bookRef.book: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry

discriminators: Timing: started or worsened within days to weeks of starting or increasing an antipsychotic (or sometimes an SSRI)?
The inner experience: 'I have to move' (akathisia) versus 'I'm afraid something bad will happen' (anxiety).
The movement: rocking from foot to foot, marching on the spot, crossing and uncrossing legs, unable to stay seated (Stahl p. 169).
Does the restlessness ease with reassurance or relaxation? Anxiety often does; akathisia often does not.

cases.vignette: Two weeks after a new antipsychotic, Deepak keeps standing up mid-sentence. 'It's not worry. My legs just won't let me stay still.' Breathing exercises make no difference.
cases.why: Timing, an urge to move without fear content, no response to relaxation (Maudsley p. 114).

cases.vignette: Before an exam, Nisha fidgets and jiggles her foot, her heart races, and she fears she will fail. On no medicine.
cases.why: Fear content, situational trigger, no medicine change.

cases.vignette: Harish paces, shouting that the neighbours are sending signals through the wall; this began before any treatment.
cases.why: Restlessness driven by psychotic content, predating medicine.

cases.vignette: Priya says she 'can't settle' in the evenings. You do not know her medicines or when it began.
cases.why: Timing relative to medicine changes is the key question.

cases.vignette: A week after his antipsychotic dose went up, Kiran says, 'I'm crawling out of my skin; I can't take this,' and rocks from foot to foot when standing.
cases.why: Recent increase, inner unease, classic rocking. Assess risk because distress is high (Maudsley p. 114).

content.whyItMatters: Mislabelled akathisia can be read as 'non-engagement' or 'worsening psychosis'. Maudsley notes the postulated link with suicidal ideation (p. 114). Naming it as a likely side effect, and passing that to the prescriber, protects the client and the alliance.

reviewFlags: Maudsley states the akathisia-suicidality association is postulated but uncertain (p. 114); antipsychotics 2.1 states it more strongly ('raises suicide risk'); align wording.
Remove 'Propranolol helps' style treatment advice from the psychologist-facing copy.

title: Stopping or slipping? Discontinuation versus relapse
objective: Use timing, symptom type and response to restarting to judge whether symptoms after stopping an antidepressant are more likely discontinuation (withdrawal) symptoms or a return of depression, and explain both possibilities to a client without alarm.

bookRef.book: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry
bookRef.chapter: Ch 3 Antidepressant withdrawal symptoms; Stopping antidepressants

rules: Withdrawal symptoms start fast, within days (within 3-5 half-lives of the drug), and ease quickly if the medicine is restarted (Maudsley p. 343).
Withdrawal often brings NEW physical or sensory symptoms the person never had with depression: dizziness (most common), 'brain zaps', nausea, flu-like feelings (Maudsley p. 343, Fig 3.3).
Short half-life drugs give symptoms within a day or two; with fluoxetine, symptoms can be delayed by 2-6 weeks (Maudsley p. 344).
Relapse usually builds over weeks and looks like the person's original episode.

cases.vignette: Two days after stopping a short-acting antidepressant, Sameer is dizzy, has electric zaps when he turns his head, and feels tearful and irritable.
cases.why: Fast onset, new sensory symptoms (Maudsley p. 343).

cases.vignette: Three months after a planned, slow stop, Leela's early-morning waking, loss of interest and guilt have crept back, just like her first episode.
cases.why: Slow return of the original pattern, long after stopping.

cases.vignette: Four weeks after stopping fluoxetine, Ajay feels unsteady and nauseous, and also low.
cases.why: Fluoxetine withdrawal can be delayed by 2-6 weeks (Maudsley p. 344), and low mood occurs in both.

cases.vignette: Ten days after stopping, Farah reports only flat mood, poor sleep and hopelessness. No physical symptoms.
cases.why: Withdrawal can include low mood (Fig 3.3), so early low mood alone is ambiguous. Screen for risk.

content.clientScript: What you are feeling may be your body adjusting to the medicine stopping. It is common and usually not dangerous, but it is not a sign of weakness or addiction. It is worth telling your doctor, who can help with how the medicine is stopped. If low mood or hopelessness grows, tell me or them straight away.

reviewFlags: antidepressants 3.2 already teaches FINISH and a one-line rule; this activity adds case discrimination and must use consistent terms.
Maudsley reports withdrawal incidence of 27-86% (weighted average 56%) (p. 344); figures are debated and should not be presented as precise.
No tapering instructions: the client script refers to the doctor for how to stop.

title: "I've stopped my lithium": an adherence conversation
objective: Respond to a client who has stopped a mood stabiliser by exploring their reasons, beliefs and values before giving information. Respect their autonomy, check safety, and agree a next step that keeps the prescriber involved.

bookRef.book: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry
bookRef.chapter: Ch 14 Enhancing medication adherence; Ch 2 Stopping lithium

content.client: Raghav, 29, software tester, bipolar I disorder, well for 18 months on lithium. He arrives saying: 'I stopped my lithium three weeks ago. I feel flat on it and I'm tired of blood tests. I'm fine now, so I don't need it.'
content.scoring: Each turn has 3 options scored: best (explores and reflects), ok (accurate but premature), harm (confronts, threatens or colludes).

options.text: You've made a big decision. Can you tell me what made you decide, and what it has been like since?
options.feedback: Opens with curiosity. People stop for reasons, and knowing them is the starting point.

options.text: Stopping lithium is risky. You need to restart it.
options.feedback: Persuading before understanding usually increases resistance.
Important later, but as an opener it can feel like checking up on him.

turns.clientSays: Feeling flat is the worst part. I used to be the funny one. And the blood tests make me feel like a patient forever.

options.text: So the medicine has cost you something that matters (feeling like yourself) and the tests are a reminder of the illness.
options.feedback: Reflects both meaning and loss. He feels heard.

options.text: Lots of people feel flat; you get used to it.
Flatness can sometimes be adjusted. Your psychiatrist could look at that.
options.feedback: True and useful, but offered before he has finished telling his story.

options.text: Since stopping, have you noticed any changes in sleep, energy, spending or how fast your thoughts go?
options.feedback: Checks for early relapse signs without lecturing. Maudsley notes abrupt stopping of psychotropics worsens outcomes (p. 898), so early warning signs matter.
A frightening prediction that damages trust.

options.text: Let's not talk about the medicine today.
Would it be OK if I shared what I know about stopping lithium, and you tell me what fits for you?
options.feedback: Asking permission keeps him in charge of the decision.

options.text: Here are the statistics on relapse after stopping.
options.feedback: Information without permission can feel like a lecture.

options.text: It's your choice, so I won't say anything.
options.feedback: Respecting autonomy does not mean withholding relevant information.

options.text: Whatever you decide, would you be willing to see your psychiatrist this week so the decision is made with full information, and we agree on signs that would mean getting help early?
options.feedback: Keeps the prescriber involved, builds a relapse-signature plan, and respects his choice. Maudsley notes NICE guidance that a capacitous person's right to decline should be respected, with concerns recorded (p. 897).

options.text: I'll call your psychiatrist and tell them you're non-compliant.
options.feedback: Labels and bypasses him; consent and confidentiality rules apply.

options.text: Just restart at your old dose tonight.
options.feedback: Dosing advice is outside a psychologist's role.

factsForDebrief: About 50% of people with long-term conditions do not take medicines as prescribed; most are partially adherent (Maudsley p. 898).
In one study, prescribers identified only half of non-adherent patients (Maudsley p. 898), so a psychologist is often the first to hear.
Many adherence-intervention studies are low quality (Maudsley p. 898); collaborative, person-specific approaches are favoured (p. 899).

reviewFlags: Planned in CURRICULUM_MAP row 136; this is the spec for it.
Do not include lithium relapse statistics unless a page-cited figure is added from Maudsley ch 2, 301 after review.
Consent and confidentiality wording should follow the ethics-law module and Indian MHCA 2017 context, not the UK Mental Health Act in Maudsley ch 14.

title: Clozapine year one: what the psychologist watches
objective: Across one year of a client's clozapine treatment, recognise the side effects and life changes that need action (infection signs, chest symptoms, constipation, hypersalivation, smoking change, metabolic change) and choose the right speed of escalation, while supporting the client's recovery goals.

bookRef.book: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry
bookRef.chapter: Ch 1 Clozapine adverse effects; Ch 11 Smoking and psychotropic drugs

content.client: Suresh, 27, treatment-resistant schizophrenia, lives with his parents in Nagpur, wants to return to his job at a print shop. Starts clozapine in hospital, then continues at home.

beats.situation: Suresh says he has had a fever and feels his heart racing even sitting still. He is breathless climbing the stairs.

choices.text: Arrange urgent same-day medical review and alert the team
choices.consequence: He is checked for myocarditis, which is most likely in the first 6-8 weeks (Maudsley p. 223).

choices.text: Suggest rest and fluids for the 'flu'
choices.consequence: Heart inflammation can be fatal (Maudsley p. 222).

choices.text: Mention it at next week's session
choices.consequence: Too slow for chest symptoms in early clozapine treatment.

beats.situation: He is calmer and the voices are quieter. His mother mentions he hardly goes to the toilet and complains of a 'heavy stomach'.

choices.text: Tell the team today and ask Suresh directly about bowel habits from now on
choices.consequence: Constipation is common and can be deadly; active questioning is advised (Maudsley p. 232-233).

choices.text: Suggest more vegetables and leave it
choices.consequence: Diet helps prevention, but the team needs to know now.

choices.text: Assume it's from inactivity
choices.consequence: Missed hypomotility has a high case fatality (Maudsley p. 232).

beats.situation: He is embarrassed about drooling at night and has skipped some evening doses.

choices.text: Normalise it, and help him tell the prescriber this week, including the missed doses
choices.consequence: Hypersalivation is manageable (Maudsley p. 227). Restarting after gaps needs medical advice (p. 207).

choices.text: Tell him to just take the morning dose
choices.consequence: Dose decisions belong to the prescriber.

choices.text: Ignore it; it's cosmetic
choices.consequence: It is driving non-adherence.

beats.situation: Motivated by your work together, he wants to quit smoking next month.

choices.text: Support the plan and help him inform the prescriber before the quit date
choices.consequence: Stopping smoking can raise clozapine levels sharply; smoking can cut levels by up to 50% (Maudsley p. 856).

choices.text: Advise him not to quit while on clozapine
choices.consequence: Quitting is a health goal; it just needs planning.

choices.text: Suggest nicotine patches so levels stay the same
choices.consequence: Nicotine replacement does not prevent the change; it is the smoke, not nicotine, that speeds up the enzyme (Maudsley p. 856).

beats.situation: He has gained weight and feels ashamed at the gym. He asks whether he should stop the 'fattening tablet'.

choices.text: Explore the impact, link him with the team's physical-health monitoring, and start behavioural work on activity and eating that he chooses
choices.consequence: Metabolic effects are common with several antipsychotics and need monitoring (Stahl p. 198-201); behaviour change is the psychologist's strength.

choices.text: Tell him weight gain is the price of recovery
choices.consequence: Dismissive; weight gain is a common reason people stop treatment.

choices.text: Agree he should stop
choices.consequence: Outside your role; abrupt stopping risks relapse.

beats.situation: He has a sore throat and fever the week before his job interview.

choices.text: Same-day contact with the clozapine team for a blood count
choices.consequence: Any infection sign on clozapine needs a same-day white cell check (Maudsley p. 222).

choices.text: Treat it as a cold; the high-risk period is over
choices.consequence: Risk is much lower after year one (Maudsley p. 222) but not zero; checking is still the rule.

reviewFlags: antipsychotics 3.1 and 3.4 cover the facts in prescriber framing (including titration); this activity is recognition-only. Reviewer should decide whether 3.4 'Titration' stays in the psychologist track.
Indian clozapine monitoring arrangements vary; localise 'clozapine team'.
Myocarditis incidence estimates vary widely between countries (Maudsley p. 222); no incidence figure used here.

title: Interaction families
objective: Match common real-life situations to the interaction family they belong to, and to the psychologist's response, without learning drug-by-drug tables.

bookRef.book: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry
bookRef.chapter: Ch 11 Pharmacokinetics (CYP function, smoking, alcohol); Ch 2 Lithium interactions; Ch 3 Antidepressant interactions; Ch 4 Street drugs

families.name: Enzyme speed changes (induction or inhibition)
families.plain: Something speeds up or slows down the liver's clearing of a medicine, so its level falls or rises (Stahl p. 49; Maudsley p. 851-852).

families.name: Smoking change
families.plain: Tobacco smoke speeds up CYP1A2; starting or stopping changes levels of medicines such as clozapine and olanzapine (Maudsley p. 856).

families.name: Sodium and fluid handling
families.plain: Anything that changes salt or water balance can raise lithium levels (Maudsley p. 251-254).

families.name: Serotonin stacking
families.plain: Two or more serotonergic medicines or substances add up and risk serotonin syndrome (Maudsley p. 337, 379).

families.name: Sedation stacking
families.plain: Alcohol, sleeping tablets, opioids and sedating medicines add together, raising risk of over-sedation, accidents and breathing problems (Maudsley p. 862-863).

pairs.situation: A client on lithium starts over-the-counter painkillers for back pain.
pairs.action: Tell the prescriber; some painkillers (NSAIDs) can raise lithium (Maudsley p. 253).

pairs.situation: A client on clozapine is admitted to a no-smoking ward.
pairs.action: Make sure the team knows smoking status changed (Maudsley p. 856).

pairs.situation: A client on an SSRI is prescribed a strong painkiller by a dentist that also acts on serotonin.
pairs.action: Suggest they tell both prescribers what they take; know serotonin syndrome warning signs.

pairs.situation: A client on a benzodiazepine says he drinks most nights to 'switch off'.
pairs.action: Explore drinking, screen risk, and share with the prescriber with consent.

pairs.situation: A client's epilepsy medicine was changed, and since then her antidepressant 'stopped working'.
pairs.action: Suggest she ask her doctors whether the new medicine affects the other; some anticonvulsants, such as carbamazepine, speed up liver enzymes (Maudsley p. 852).

pairs.situation: A client using MDMA at weekends is also on an SSRI.
pairs.action: Non-judgemental harm-reduction conversation; inform prescriber with consent (Maudsley p. 526-527; serotonin syndrome risk p. 337).

pairs.situation: A client on lithium has been vomiting with a stomach bug for two days.
pairs.action: Same-day medical review: fluid loss raises lithium (Maudsley p. 251).

content.principle: You do not need to know every interaction. Ask about every medicine, supplement, substance and smoking change, and tell the prescriber when something changes.

reviewFlags: Overlaps medicine-profiles 3.3 'Dangerous combinations'; this groups them by mechanism family rather than listing them. Check for duplicate pairs.
Lithium-and-stomach-bug pair duplicates the 'summer of lithium' scenario; keep it only as reinforcement or swap it.
MDMA pair touches substance use: tone should match the substance module's harm-reduction stance.

title: Special groups sorter
objective: Match medicine-related concerns to pregnancy and the postpartum period, older adults, or children and young people, and state the monitoring or conversation point the psychologist should hold for each.

bookRef.book: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry
bookRef.chapter: Part 2: Ch 5 Children and adolescents; Ch 6 Older people; Ch 7 Pregnancy and breastfeeding

cards.concern: Stopping medicine suddenly can be risky too, and untreated illness also affects the baby; both belong in the conversation.
cards.point: Support a joint decision with the prescriber; do not endorse abrupt stopping (Maudsley p. 681).

cards.concern: Risks should be explained as natural frequencies ('1 in 100') rather than percentages.
cards.point: A communication skill psychologists can model (Maudsley p. 681).

cards.concern: Around one in five women with bipolar disorder have a psychotic relapse after birth.
cards.point: Plan early-warning signs before delivery (Maudsley p. 681).

cards.concern: The body handles drugs differently as pregnancy goes on, so medicine plans may need review.
cards.point: Encourage regular prescriber contact through pregnancy (Maudsley p. 681).

cards.concern: Greater sensitivity to sedatives, more falls, slower response to antidepressants.
cards.point: Ask about falls, confusion and sleepiness after any change (Maudsley p. 601).

cards.concern: Antipsychotics for distress in dementia carry stroke risk and are reviewed carefully.
cards.point: Offer non-drug approaches for behavioural symptoms; monitor (Maudsley p. 601, 644).

cards.concern: Medicines hidden in food or drink raise legal and ethical questions.
cards.point: Covert administration requires a formal capacity and best-interests process (Maudsley p. 667); raise ethics concerns with the team.

cards.concern: Early on, SSRIs carry a small increased risk of suicidal thinking, while untreated depression also carries risk.
cards.point: Close risk monitoring in the first weeks; involve carers (Maudsley p. 545).

cards.concern: Treatment targets symptoms more than diagnostic labels, and side effects are more common.
cards.point: Help track target symptoms and side effects week to week (Maudsley p. 539).

reviewFlags: Covert administration law differs between India (MHCA 2017) and England; ethics-law module owner to review card 7.
stabilisers 1.6 and antidepressants 2.6 cover the drug-specific risks; this activity is about monitoring and conversation, so check for duplication.

title: "Nothing works": checking before calling it resistant
objective: Before accepting that a client's illness is 'treatment-resistant', identify the factors a psychologist can check and contribute (diagnosis, adherence, substances, psychological treatment dose, physical illness, ongoing stressors), and describe treatment resistance as a concept without recommending medicines.

bookRef.book: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry
bookRef.chapter: Ch 3 Treatment-resistant depression; Ch 1 Refractory schizophrenia; Ch 14 Adherence

additionalRefs.chapter: Ch 7 Treatment resistance in unipolar depression

content.client: Meenal, 44, school administrator, depressed for two years. She says, 'I've tried three tablets. Nothing works. I'm a hopeless case.'

choices.text: Map her treatment story: what was tried, for how long, and how she actually took it
choices.consequence: Adequacy and adherence are the first checks; partial adherence is common and often hidden (Maudsley p. 898).

choices.text: Agree she is treatment-resistant and focus on acceptance
choices.consequence: Premature, and it reinforces hopelessness.

choices.text: Suggest she asks for ECT
choices.consequence: Treatment choice is not the psychologist's call and is premature.

beats.situation: She admits she often stopped each tablet after 10 days because of nausea.

choices.text: Reflect that these may not have been full trials, and help her share this openly with her psychiatrist
choices.consequence: Pseudo-resistance: short or partial trials are not true failures.

choices.text: Tell her she sabotaged her treatment
choices.consequence: Shaming reduces honesty.

beats.situation: Screening reveals nightly drinking since her divorce and untreated hypothyroidism symptoms.

choices.text: Address drinking collaboratively and encourage a medical check of physical causes; share both with the team with consent
choices.consequence: Substance use and physical illness are classic contributors to apparent resistance.

choices.text: Focus only on mood
choices.consequence: Misses modifiable factors.

beats.situation: She has never had a structured psychological therapy.

choices.text: Offer an evidence-based therapy at a full dose of sessions as part of the plan
choices.consequence: Combined treatment is the norm; therapy 'dose' matters as much as drug dose.

choices.text: Wait until the medicine works
choices.consequence: Delays an effective treatment.

content.conceptCard: Treatment resistance is a concept for when adequate, properly taken treatments have not helped. The prescriber decides on medical next steps (for schizophrenia, Maudsley discusses clozapine for refractory illness, p. 190). The psychologist's role is to make sure the 'adequate and properly taken' parts are true, and to keep hope realistic.

reviewFlags: antidepressants 3.4 already teaches pseudo-resistance and adherence checks; this case is the applied version. Keep its 'Then the options' prescriber content out of the psychologist track.
Avoid any definitional numbers (e.g., number of failed trials) unless page-cited; Maudsley's TRD definitions (p. 317) to be checked by reviewer if added.
